theory.overview: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the brain of the computer—the component that executes instructions and orchestrates all computation. Modern CPUs are marvels of engineering, containing billions of transistors that implement instruction fetching, decoding, execution, and coordination with memory and I/O. Understanding CPU architecture reveals how software instructions transform into electrical signals that manipulate data. From the classic von Neumann architecture to modern superscalar out-of-order designs, the evolution of CPUs represents the relentless pursuit of performance within the constraints of physics.

sections.title: Von Neumann Architecture: The Foundation
sections.content: The dominant computer organization, named after John von Neumann, stores both instructions and data in the same memory. The CPU fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, executes them, and writes results back. This stored-program concept enables flexibility—the same hardware runs different programs by loading different instruction sequences into memory. The architecture consists of: CPU (ALU + control unit + registers), memory, and I/O interfaces.

sections.title: The Datapath: Where Computation Happens
sections.content: The datapath contains the functional units that process data: ALU for arithmetic/logic, shifters for bit manipulation, registers for temporary storage, and buses that connect everything. Data flows from registers through the ALU and back to registers. The control unit orchestrates this flow by generating signals that open/close data paths at the right times. A well-designed datapath enables efficient instruction execution.

sections.title: Control Unit: The Conductor
sections.content: The control unit directs all processor operations. It fetches instructions, decodes them to determine what actions to take, and generates control signals that activate the appropriate datapath elements. Control can be hardwired (fast, fixed) or microprogrammed (flexible, slower). Modern CPUs use hardwired control for common operations with microcode for complex instructions.

sections.title: Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
sections.content: The ISA defines the interface between hardware and software—the instructions the CPU understands, registers available, memory model, and I/O operations. ISAs can be CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) like x86 with many powerful instructions, or RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) like ARM or RISC-V with simple, uniform instructions. The ISA is the contract: software compiled for an ISA runs on any compatible hardware implementation.

sections.title: Pipelining: Assembly Line Execution
sections.content: Pipelining overlaps instruction execution stages—while one instruction executes, the next is decoded, and another is fetched. A classic 5-stage pipeline: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback. Pipelining ideally achieves one instruction per clock cycle (IPC = 1), dramatically improving throughput. However, hazards (data dependencies, branches, structural conflicts) can stall the pipeline.
stages: ID - Instruction Decode and register read
WB - Write result back to register

sections.title: Modern CPU Features
sections.content: High-performance CPUs employ sophisticated techniques: superscalar execution (multiple instructions per cycle), out-of-order execution (execute when ready, not in order), speculative execution (predict and execute branches before knowing outcome), and branch prediction (guess branch direction to avoid stalls). These features extract instruction-level parallelism from sequential programs.

keyConcepts.name: Stored-Program Concept
keyConcepts.description: Instructions stored as data in memory, allowing the same hardware to run different programs.

keyConcepts.name: IPC (Instructions Per Cycle)
keyConcepts.description: Average instructions completed per clock cycle. Ideal pipelined CPU achieves IPC = 1.

keyConcepts.name: CPI (Cycles Per Instruction)
keyConcepts.description: Average clock cycles needed per instruction. Inverse of IPC.

keyConcepts.name: Hazard
keyConcepts.description: Situation preventing next instruction from executing in its designated cycle.

steps.title: Fetch Instruction
steps.description: Read instruction from memory address in PC, then increment PC.

steps.title: Decode Instruction
steps.description: Determine operation type and which registers to use.

steps.title: Execute Operation
steps.description: ALU performs the operation on source operands.

steps.title: Write Back Result
steps.description: Store ALU result in destination register.

practiceProblems.title: Von Neumann Feature
practiceProblems.description: What is the key feature of von Neumann architecture?
practiceProblems.explanation: The von Neumann architecture stores both instructions and data in the same memory, enabling the stored-program concept where programs are data that can be loaded and executed.
hints: Same memory for code and data

practiceProblems.title: ISA Purpose
practiceProblems.description: What does ISA stand for and what is its purpose?
practiceProblems.answer: Instruction Set Architecture - interface between hardware and software
practiceProblems.explanation: The ISA defines the instructions, registers, and operations that software can use. It abstracts hardware implementation details from programmers.

practiceProblems.title: Pipeline Stages
practiceProblems.description: What are the classic 5 pipeline stages?
practiceProblems.explanation: The 5 stages are: IF (Instruction Fetch), ID (Instruction Decode), EX (Execute), MEM (Memory access), WB (Write Back).

practiceProblems.title: CPI Calculation
practiceProblems.description: If a CPU executes 1 billion instructions in 2 billion cycles, what is the CPI?
practiceProblems.explanation: CPI = Cycles / Instructions = 2 billion / 1 billion = 2. On average, each instruction takes 2 cycles.

practiceProblems.title: RISC vs CISC
practiceProblems.description: Which typically has more registers: RISC or CISC?
practiceProblems.explanation: RISC architectures typically have more registers (e.g., ARM has 16-32, RISC-V has 32) compared to CISC (x86 has 8 general-purpose).
hints: CISC like x86 has fewer registers

practiceProblems.title: Superscalar Execution
practiceProblems.description: What is the maximum theoretical IPC for a 4-wide superscalar processor?
practiceProblems.explanation: A 4-wide superscalar can issue up to 4 instructions per cycle, achieving maximum IPC of 4 (assuming perfect instruction mix and no dependencies).

minigame.title: CPU Commander
minigame.description: Control a CPU's execution! Manage the datapath, coordinate pipeline stages, handle hazards, and maximize instruction throughput. Build the ultimate processing machine!
instructions: Instructions arrive and need to flow through pipeline stages
Handle data hazards by stalling or forwarding
Predict branches to avoid pipeline flushes
Keep all pipeline stages busy for maximum throughput!

snippets.title: Simple CPU Simulation
snippets.code:
class SimpleCPU:
    def __init__(self):
        self.registers = [0] * 8
        self.pc = 0
        self.memory = [0] * 256
        self.running = True
        self.cycles = 0
    
    def load_program(self, program):
        for i, instr in enumerate(program):
            self.memory[i] = instr
    
    def fetch(self):
        instr = self.memory[self.pc]
        self.pc = (self.pc + 1) % 256
        return instr
    
    def decode_execute(self, instr):
        opcode = (instr >> 6) & 0x3
        rd = (instr >> 3) & 0x7
        rs = instr & 0x7
        
        if opcode == 0:  # ADD
            self.registers[rd] = (self.registers[rd] + self.registers[rs]) & 0xFF
        elif opcode == 1:  # SUB
            self.registers[rd] = (self.registers[rd] - self.registers[rs]) & 0xFF
        elif opcode == 2:  # LOAD
            addr = self.registers[rs]
            self.registers[rd] = self.memory[addr]
        elif opcode == 3:  # STORE
            addr = self.registers[rs]
            self.memory[addr] = self.registers[rd]
        
        self.cycles += 1
    
    def run(self, max_cycles=100):
        while self.running and self.cycles < max_cycles:
            instr = self.fetch()
            if instr == 0:
                break
            self.decode_execute(instr)
    
    def dump(self):
        print(f'PC: {self.pc}, Cycles: {self.cycles}')
        print(f'Registers: {self.registers}')

# Test program: R0 = 5 + 3 = 8
# ADD R0, R1: opcode=0, rd=0, rs=1
cpu = SimpleCPU()
cpu.registers[0] = 5
cpu.registers[1] = 3
program = [0b000001000]  # ADD R0, R1
cpu.load_program(program)
cpu.run()
cpu.dump()
